research_program: Copy-aware Paged KV management and adaptive execution for commodity single-GPU llama.cpp serving

claims.question: When does 128-bit vectorization reduce the cost of snapshot-preserving KV Remap?
claims.hypothesis: With identical descriptors and snapshot semantics, uint4 Gather/Scatter reduces GPU time relative to scalar Remap for aligned FP16 KV, with the largest relative effect at small block counts and diminishing benefit as memory traffic dominates.
confounders: GPU clock, temperature, and WDDM scheduling
claims.mechanism: Each aligned thread moves eight FP16 elements through one uint4 load/store, reducing descriptor-loop and instruction overhead; as transfers grow, bandwidth and staging traffic bound the attainable gain.
falsification: Any preregistered block count has paired median GPU regression above 3%.
No preregistered block count reaches 10% paired median GPU improvement.
The vector path changes output, violates snapshot semantics, or produces sanitizer errors.
Production application evidence records no vectorized bytes while claiming that the path is used.
observed_results: Twenty paired alternating-order trials measured 53.33%, 48.89%, 3.13%, and 1.87% median GPU improvement for 1, 4, 16, and 32 blocks.
The real application journey recorded 5,603,330 vectorized Remap bytes.
These results are operator-level evidence and do not establish end-to-end serving acceleration.
scope_limits: RTX 4050 Laptop GPU, sm_89, Windows WDDM
FP16 KV with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, 16-token blocks
KV movement operator only; not Paged Decode Attention
claims.negative_result_policy: Retain regressions by block count, alignment, and fallback fraction; do not average them into a positive headline.

claims.question: Under which workload and layout regimes does explicit KV movement materially affect decode service outcomes?
claims.hypothesis: Explicit KV movement becomes material as moved bytes, fragmentation, shared-prefix COW, and memory pressure increase, but scheduler-induced queueing can dominate or reverse the operator-level effect.
independent_variables: context length and moved KV bytes
batch shape, arrival process, and memory pressure
dependent_metrics: TTFT, TPOT/TBT, queue latency, request P95, and throughput
resident sequence capacity and fallback count
confounders: GPU power, clock, and thermal state
claims.mechanism: More explicit movement consumes device bandwidth and launches, while fragmentation and snapshot semantics determine whether Direct is legal; request scheduling can amplify or hide this cost through queue structure.
falsification: Profiler evidence shows KV movement is immaterial in every preregistered high-copy or high-pressure regime.
Reducing movement does not change kernel time, admissible capacity, or request outcomes beyond uncertainty in any regime.
Apparent request gains occur without a corresponding scheduler or CUDA mediator.
scope_limits: No occupancy, roofline, or memory-bound claim until Nsight evidence exists
claims.negative_result_policy: Publish regimes where non-KV compute or queueing dominates and narrow the research question instead of relabeling noise as a gain.

claims.question: When is restricted Paged Decode Attention preferable to Direct or explicit KV Remap?
claims.hypothesis: Direct page-table reads can avoid materialization bytes and improve capacity or latency only beyond a context, fragmentation, or reuse frontier; indirect addressing and online-softmax overhead may make it slower for short or contiguous cases.
independent_variables: Direct, Remap, or Paged Decode action
context length, page size, and physical fragmentation
prefix reuse and resident sequence count
dependent_metrics: attention output error versus contiguous oracle
CUDA-event kernel time and device bytes
peak KV memory and admissible batch
TTFT, TPOT/TBT, request P95, and throughput
confounders: different attention math, masking, or precision
layout conversion outside the timed region
claims.mechanism: Paged Decode removes full-cache materialization but adds block-table lookup, irregular memory access, masking, online softmax, and reduction costs; the winning action depends on avoided bytes and available concurrency.
falsification: The restricted kernel fails the numerical oracle or memory-safety checks.
It is neither non-inferior in latency nor beneficial in resident capacity in every preregistered regime.
Any measured gain disappears when layout conversion and warm-up are controlled.
The implementation silently falls back while metrics claim Paged execution.
scope_limits: Qwen2.5, FP16 KV, GQA, head dimension 128
Single consumer NVIDIA GPU; unsupported shapes must fall back
claims.negative_result_policy: Report the losing regions and capacity/latency trade-off; a slower kernel with a measured capacity benefit is not rewritten as a latency win.

claims.question: Can an explainable cost model safely select among KV execution actions better than a fixed rule?
claims.hypothesis: A model using measurable movement, fragmentation, reuse, memory-pressure, and compute features can reduce paired regret relative to the fixed rule while bounding wrong enables and decision overhead.
independent_variables: fixed rule versus analytical, table-driven, learned, or hybrid policy
available action set and safety thresholds
dependent_metrics: TTFT, TPOT/TBT, request P95, throughput, and memory pressure
confounders: trace leakage between training and evaluation
claims.mechanism: No single action minimizes cost across copy legality, bytes, fragmentation, memory pressure, and decode work; an uncertainty-aware policy should choose only when predicted benefit exceeds risk and overhead.
falsification: The policy exceeds preregistered paired-regret or upstream-regression gates.
Decision overhead removes the selected action's benefit.
The policy continues harmful actions after a registered distribution shift.
A fixed rule matches or beats it across all held-out regimes within uncertainty.
scope_limits: The present Ridge Benefit Gate selects scheduling plans, not the future five-action KV policy.
Held-out evaluation is restricted to the available single-GPU workload matrix
claims.negative_result_policy: Keep the fixed rule when it is statistically indistinguishable or safer; publish misprediction regimes and fallback behavior.

claims.question: Can a scheduling decision change CUDA work yet harm request latency despite reducing aggregate engine execution time?
claims.hypothesis: Policy interventions affect request outcomes through scheduler shape and CUDA KV work, and phase aggregates are insufficient because changed batching and queue order can reverse TTFT.
independent_variables: forced upstream versus forced CacheFlow policy
dependent_metrics: KV launches, copied bytes, and CUDA-event time
claims.mechanism: More chunks and changed batch order alter queue waiting while adding KV work; aggregate execute duration omits how work is distributed across requests.
falsification: The intervention changes no scheduling decision.
Scheduling changes occur without a material CUDA mediator.
CUDA changes occur without a material request-level outcome.
The effect vanishes under paired trials and is attributable only to sampling noise.
observed_results: Three paired Latin interventions recorded +13 CacheFlow decisions, +23 prefill chunks, -354 prefill tokens, +2 custom KV launches, +20,066,300 copied bytes, and +0.808 ms CUDA-event time.
Engine execute aggregate decreased by 11,446 us while TTFT P95 worsened by 85.61 ms.
The current 100 ms activity sampling is not an Nsight kernel census.
scope_limits: Three paired trials on one laptop GPU
Causal chain for the tested forced-policy workload only
No occupancy, roofline, or universal scheduler conclusion
claims.negative_result_policy: Treat harmful TTFT as a primary result and require future policies to explain or avoid it; never substitute phase aggregates for request metrics.
